claude_stage1_error: Stage 1 applied Arizona's 200% gross limit to all 12 months of 2026 and got 12 × $24 = $288. It said it could not confirm when the 200% standard took effect. Arizona used a 185% ECE standard before 200%: the CNAP manual has an archived '185% of Federal Poverty Level (Expanded Categorical Eligibility)' page, and DB101 Arizona gives 185% ($2,414 for one person) for October 1, 2025 – September 30, 2026. The household's gross income (about $2,539) is above that 185% limit. So in the months before the 200% standard (January–February 2026, per the engine's March start) the household is not categorically eligible, and the $58,700 bank balance fails the $4,500 elderly/disabled resource limit. Those months pay $0, which gives $240, not $288. Stage 1's other steps are correct: categorical eligibility waives the asset and net-income tests, the formula benefit is $0, the $24 minimum applies to eligible one-person households, and FY2026 parameters run through December under the freeze.
claude_summary: The household is one person, 80 and disabled, with about $2,539–$2,545 a month in gross income. That is above 185% of the poverty guideline ($2,413/mo) but below 200% ($2,608/mo). When Arizona's expanded categorical eligibility (ECE) limit is 200%, the household is categorically eligible, so there is no asset or net-income test. As an eligible one-person household it gets the $24 FY2026 minimum, even though its formula benefit is $0. Arizona's manual moved from a 185% ECE standard (now archived) to 200% during FY2026, after a 185% table that ran from October 2025. For the months still under 185%, the household fails the $4,500 elderly/disabled resource test and the net-income test, so it gets $0. Ten months × $24 = $240, which is the engine's own result and stands.

I agree with the engine and with stage 1. The veterans benefits are exempt from tax, so West Virginia AGI is the spouse's $88,928 of wages. Subtracting two $2,000 personal exemptions leaves $84,928 of taxable income. Enrolled SB 392 adds W. Va. Code §11-21-4j, which applies to taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026; it passed March 14, 2026, before the freeze. Under it, the tax is $1,950.50 + 4.58% × $24,928 ≈ $3,092.20. No nonrefundable credits apply. The engine reached $3,092.19 by the same steps; it carried AGI as $88,927.65, a $0.35 float artifact worth about one cent of tax. The models' $3,255.03 used the 2025 §11-21-4i rates (2.22% to 4.82%), which SB 392 replaced for 2026.

Under R&TC §17052, the only refundable California credit this childless 28-year-old can get is CalEITC. YCTC needs a child under 6, FYTC needs former-foster-youth status (unlisted, so false), and the renter's credit is nonrefundable. Federal AGI of about $22,534 is higher than earned income, so the phase-out runs on AGI. The last published amounts before the freeze are FTB's 2025 figures: $302 maximum, a $32,900 income limit, and the slow §17052(o) tail. At this AGI they give about $95, and the engine's $95.15 matches. The 2026 CCPI indexing (3.4%) was only announced in FTB Tax News after 2026-07-03, so the reference rests on frozen law and the $0 consensus is wrong: the 403(b) distribution is not disqualifying investment income, and the childless tail runs out to about $32,900.

The law supports the $288 reference. The pregnant head is a one-person SNAP household (an unborn child doesn't count). Her countable gross income is $2,083.33/mo: $1,083.33 of wages plus $1,000 of financial assistance counted as cash contributions, with the educational assistance exempt under Texas Works Handbook A-1322.1. That is under Texas's 165%-of-poverty limit for broad-based categorical eligibility ($2,152 in FY2026 and $2,194.50 for Oct–Dec), and her $190 in assets is under the $5,000 resource limit. Categorically eligible households skip the gross and net income tests. Net income of about $1,658 makes 30% of income ($498) larger than the $298 maximum, so the federal one- and two-person minimum of $24 applies each month, and 12 × $24 = $288. The engine's steps match this. The $0 consensus comes mostly from applying the federal 130% gross-income test that Texas's categorical eligibility displaces, from leaving out the minimum benefit, or from counting the exempt educational assistance. The FY2027 $25 minimum came out in August 2026, after the freeze, so $24 holds for every month.

claude_engine_step_at_issue: Colorado sales tax refund: the engine computed $19 from modified AGI of $4,625.40 using the TY2025 refund table (single, $52,000 or less, $19), as if a TABOR refund were owed for TY2026.
claude_summary: The law gives $0 in Colorado refundable credits for this filer in 2026. The head is 66 and childless, so there is no federal EITC and therefore no Colorado EITC. There is also no CTC, FATC or child care credit, and the Senior Housing Credit was not extended. The TABOR sales tax refund under C.R.S. 39-22-2003 is paid only when there is excess revenue in the fiscal year ending in the tax year (FY 2025-26), and the pre-freeze forecasts project revenue below the Referendum C cap with no income-tax-form refunds. The engine's $19 is exactly the TY2025 DR 0104 single-filer amount for modified AGI of $52,000 or less, carried into 2026 when no 2026 refund was owed or published.

The Michigan Homestead Property Tax Credit is a state income tax credit, and any amount above the tax liability is paid to the claimant. For a renter, 23% of gross rent counts as property tax: 0.23 × $10,560 = $2,428.80. A claimant who is not a senior gets 60% of the amount by which that exceeds 3.2% of total household resources (THR = $36,276): 0.6 × ($2,428.80 − $1,160.83) = $760.78. The 2025 maximum credit ($1,900) and phase-out limits ($62,500 to $71,500) do not bind. The Michigan EITC and Home Heating Credit are both $0. The engine did the same steps and got $760.79. The 1-cent gap is a float artifact, because the engine used THR = $36,275.59. Its 'household resource exemption of $1,267.98' is really the excess above the 3.2% threshold, which is mislabeled but correctly applied. The 0 consensus misses the renter's homestead credit, or counts only the part refunded above liability, whereas the definition asks for the total refundable credit amount.

Va. Code § 58.1-339.8(3) lets a filer claim a refundable credit for taxable years 2025 and 2026. The credit equals 20% of the federal § 32 EITC and is taken in place of the nonrefundable low-income credit and the nonrefundable EITC. The head is 40 and has no children, so the federal EITC is 7.65% × $520 = $39.78, which gives $7.96 for Virginia. The engine's steps match this, and stage 1 reached the same figure. The consensus answer of $0 rests on the wrong belief that the credit is nonrefundable or has expired. The only open point is rounding: the IRS lookup table gives an EITC of $40, which would make the Virginia credit $8.00.

Head is a one-person SNAP household that receives Social Security disability benefits, so Head counts as a disabled member. Monthly gross income is about $2,146, under Michigan's 200% FPL categorical-eligibility limit of $2,610, and Michigan has no FAP asset test at or below 200% FPL. On every reading of the medical deduction, the computed allotment ($298 − 30% of net income) is negative. Federal law and Michigan BEM 213 still give one- and two-person categorically eligible groups the minimum benefit, which is $24/month for FY2026, so 12 × $24 = $288. The engine follows exactly this path; its net income of $1,755 differs slightly from stage 1's $1,747, which does not change the result. The $0 consensus overlooks the minimum-benefit rule.

Under the law published by the freeze, the couple's monthly gross income is $1,511: $630 of SSDI plus $881 of SSI ($1,491 couple rate minus $610 countable). Arizona's net $145 standard medical deduction applies because their medical costs are at least $36 a month. With the FY2026 $209 standard deduction, net income is $1,157. 30% of that rounds up to $348, and $546 − $348 = $198 a month, or $2,376 a year. The engine's steps match this exactly. The FY2027 COLA ($562/$217) is dated 2026-08-21, after the freeze, so keeping the FY2026 amounts for Oct–Dec is correct. The $1,956 consensus deducts only the actual $26 excess medical cost and misses Arizona's standard medical deduction.

Alabama taxes interest on other states' bonds even though that interest is federally tax-exempt. It exempts only interest on U.S. obligations and on Alabama or Alabama local obligations, plus Social Security. The prompt does not say the bonds are Alabama obligations, and it tells models to treat unlisted facts as false, so the $4,734 is Alabama AGI. Subtracting the $3,000 single standard deduction (AGI under $26,000) and the $1,500 personal exemption leaves $234, taxed at 2% = $4.68. The engine took the same path. It also built an itemized medical figure from about $2,585 of medical costs, apparently an imputed Medicare Part B premium plus the $150. That figure plus the employee business expense deduction is still below $3,000, so the standard deduction applies and the result is unchanged. The 0 consensus rests on the mistaken idea that Alabama exempts all federally tax-exempt interest, or on overstated deductions (Alabama has no extra 65+ standard deduction).
